paragraphs: Rendering a scene with 3D Gaussian splatting can require millions of Gaussian primitives. Removing some of these primitives reduces the representation size, but rendering speed does not necessarily improve proportionally. This paper identifies an overlooked reason: each Gaussian can cover many pixels, and those individual contributions, called fragments, also determine the rendering workload.

The proposed method prunes fragments within individual Gaussians. It dynamically optimizes a separate pruning threshold for each Gaussian, allowing the renderer to discard selected pixel contributions. Because this operates within primitives, it can complement methods that remove whole Gaussians. The approach therefore targets a different source of computation from the primitive count alone.

Experiments cover both static and dynamic scenes. Combined with existing Gaussian pruning methods, fragment pruning achieves up to a 1.71-fold rendering speedup on the Jetson Orin NX edge GPU. The authors also report an average improvement of 0.16 PSNR on Tanks&Temples. These results show that reducing fragment work can improve practical rendering efficiency while also improving measured image quality in the reported evaluation.
neurips-2024-3d-gaussian-rendering-can-b.tldr: Learning which pixel contributions to prune from each Gaussian accelerates rendering and complements methods that remove entire Gaussians.

paragraphs: A language agent must often turn a complex request into smaller tasks whose order depends on one another. This paper represents that structure as a graph: nodes are subtasks, and edges describe dependencies. Planning then becomes the problem of selecting and executing a connected path or subgraph that fulfills the request.

The authors investigate whether graph learning can improve this process. Their theoretical analysis identifies biases in attention and the autoregressive training loss that hinder LLM decision-making on graphs. This motivates combining an LLM with a graph neural network, whose handling of graph structure addresses the identified difficulties. The proposed direction changes how the planning structure is processed, alongside the separate question of how prompts are written.

In the reported experiments, GNN-based methods outperform existing solutions even without training, and a small amount of training improves them further. Their advantage grows as the task graph becomes larger. The findings suggest that explicitly processing dependencies can be particularly useful when an agent must navigate more extensive collections of interdependent subtasks.
neurips-2024-can-graph-learning-improve-.tldr: Combining graph neural networks with LLMs improves task planning in experiments, with larger gains on larger task graphs.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning places unusual demands on an optimizer. The learning conditions change over time, the agent can lose its ability to adapt, and it must keep exploring to avoid settling prematurely on poor behavior. This paper asks whether an update rule learned specifically with these difficulties in mind can improve training.

The proposed method, OPEN, meta-learns the rule used to update an agent's parameters. Its inputs and output structure draw on earlier approaches to non-stationarity, loss of plasticity, and exploration. This gives the learned optimizer ways to respond to those issues within a single parameterization. The authors also show that the design can use randomness to support exploration across diverse learning contexts.

When meta-trained on individual environments or small collections of environments, OPEN matches or exceeds traditionally used optimizers in the reported experiments. It also shows strong generalization across a range of environments and agent architectures. These findings support learned optimization as a way to address several reinforcement-learning difficulties together, with evidence extending beyond the particular environment or architecture used for meta-training.
neurips-2024-can-learned-optimization-ma.tldr: OPEN learns an optimizer designed around reinforcement learning's changing conditions, adaptation needs, and exploration demands.

paragraphs: Graph-based semi-supervised learning uses a graph to make predictions when only some examples have labels. Existing Laplace learning methods can produce degenerate predictions when labels are scarce or classes are imbalanced, particularly around class boundaries. CutSSL approaches this problem through graph partitioning, making the assignment of examples to groups central to the formulation.

The framework starts from a minimum-cut partitioning problem with constraints on group sizes. The authors derive an exact quadratic relaxation and formulate learning as continuous, nonconvex quadratic optimization. Although the optimization uses continuous variables, they prove that the framework obtains integer solutions. This connects a continuous optimization method to the discrete assignments required for partitioning the graph.

The paper also relates its formulation to an optimization problem approximately solved by mean-shifted Laplace learning, offering insight into that existing heuristic. Across nearest-neighbor graphs and large real-world graph benchmarks, CutSSL substantially outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods under varied label rates, class imbalance, and label imbalance. The results support the partitioning formulation across several challenging labeling conditions.
neurips-2024-continuous-partitioning-for.tldr: CutSSL uses a continuous graph-partitioning formulation with provably integer solutions to improve learning with scarce or imbalanced labels.

paragraphs: A single error rate can hide which mistakes a model makes. This matters when different mistakes have different consequences, especially if those consequences change over time. The paper develops a PAC-Bayes generalization guarantee that controls probabilities across multiple error categories, providing a richer certificate than one scalar performance measure.

The bound controls the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the observed probabilities of M error types and their true probabilities. For regression, those categories can be ranges of loss values. For classification, they can correspond to entries of a confusion matrix or groups of entries. The authors also convert the bound into a differentiable objective, making it usable as a training criterion.

The central benefit is flexibility in assigning importance to errors. Earlier bounds considered here control a particular weighting chosen in advance. By bounding the error distribution, the new result implicitly controls all possible weightings simultaneously. A change in the relative severity of mistakes can therefore be considered within the same distribution-level guarantee, rather than being tied to the original weighting.
neurips-2024-controlling-multiple-errors.tldr: A new PAC-Bayes bound controls multiple error probabilities together, implicitly covering every weighting of those errors.

paragraphs: Intent-based recommendation tries to infer the purposes behind a user's behavior so that recommendations better reflect what the user wants. Existing methods can require cumbersome alternating optimization. ELCRec combines behavior representation and intent clustering in one trainable framework, allowing both to improve together using mini-batches of user data.

The method encodes user behavior sequences and represents latent intents as learnable cluster centers. Its clustering module separates those centers while drawing behavior embeddings toward them. These two pressures aim to distinguish different intents and connect observed behavior to the corresponding intent representations. An additional contrastive-learning component uses the cluster centers as self-supervision signals to strengthen this interaction.

The authors support the method with experiments and theoretical analysis. On the Beauty dataset, ELCRec improves NDCG@5 by 8.9% over the runner-up while reducing computational costs by 22.5%. They also report promising results from deployment in an industrial recommendation system with 130 million page views. Together, the reported findings connect the unified training design to improvements in recommendation performance and computational efficiency.
neurips-2024-end-to-end-learnable-cluste.tldr: ELCRec jointly learns user behavior representations and intent clusters, improving recommendation performance and reducing computational costs in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Boundary detection identifies the times when a time series changes from one class to another. Methods based on learned representations often look for differences in the distances between consecutive representations. That emphasis can become unreliable when a transition happens gradually, because the relevant change unfolds over a sequence rather than appearing as a sharp local difference.

RECURVE treats the sequence of representations as a trajectory through representation space. It computes the curvature of that trajectory at each timestamp and uses curvature as its change metric. This shifts attention from the size of consecutive movements to the trajectory's bending behavior, providing a way to accommodate both gradual and abrupt class transitions.

Using random-walk theory, the authors formally establish that mean curvature is lower near boundaries than at other points. This theoretical result supplies the basis for the proposed detection signal. Experiments across diverse real-world time-series datasets show RECURVE outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support trajectory curvature as a useful source of boundary information beyond consecutive-distance differences.
neurips-2024-exploiting-representation-c.tldr: RECURVE detects time-series class boundaries using representation-trajectory curvature, accommodating both gradual and abrupt transitions.

paragraphs: EVA learns an animatable human avatar from a single-camera RGB video, with particular attention to hands and facial expressions. These fine details are central to expressiveness but difficult to capture in this setting. The method combines 3D Gaussians with SMPL-X, an expressive parametric human model, to recover a detailed representation that can be driven.

The first contribution improves alignment between SMPL-X and the video frames. The authors introduce a reconstruction module to address weaknesses in estimating SMPL-X parameters from in-the-wild footage. Better alignment gives avatar learning a closer correspondence between the human model and the observed images, supporting the recovery of fine appearance details.

Two additional mechanisms guide Gaussian optimization. Context-aware density control adjusts gradient thresholds to account for different levels of detail across body parts, while a feedback mechanism predicts confidence for individual pixels. Experiments on two benchmarks report improvements in both quantitative measures and visual quality, especially for hands and faces. The results support combining better alignment with body-part-sensitive density control and pixel-level confidence when learning expressive avatars from monocular video.
neurips-2024-expressive-gaussian-human-a.tldr: EVA improves human avatars learned from monocular video through better model alignment, adaptive Gaussian density control, and pixel-level confidence.

paragraphs: 3D Gaussian splatting provides fast, high-quality rendering for static scenes, but extending its explicit representation to moving scenes can increase training and rendering costs. Ex4DGS addresses this by separating static and dynamic Gaussians during training. Only the dynamic Gaussians need the additional representation of motion over time.

For each dynamic Gaussian, the method explicitly samples positions and rotations at sparse timestamps. Interpolation between those samples represents motion continuously in space and time while reducing computation. Training begins with short time spans and progressively extends them, helping the method work with a small number of point clouds. A point-backtracking procedure measures accumulated error over time so that erroneous Gaussians can be detected and removed.

These choices combine an explicit motion representation with mechanisms intended to improve convergence. Experiments across various scenes report state-of-the-art rendering quality and a rendering rate of 62 frames per second on a single 2080Ti GPU. The findings demonstrate that sparse motion samples and interpolation can support detailed dynamic-scene rendering without representing every moment independently.
neurips-2024-fully-explicit-dynamic-gaus.tldr: Ex4DGS represents dynamic Gaussian motion through sparse position and rotation samples, enabling high-quality rendering at a reported 62 frames per second.

paragraphs: This paper studies what graph neural networks can compute. Its scope includes networks following the GNN architecture beyond the commonly studied aggregate-and-combine variants. The goal is a precise characterization of computational expressivity: identifying the computations available to these networks through a correspondence with another mathematical model.

The authors establish an exact correspondence with arithmetic circuits over real numbers. In that correspondence, a neural network's activation function becomes a type of gate in the circuit. This makes the choice of activation part of the computational characterization. Diverse activations can be treated within the same framework by matching them to their corresponding circuit operations.

The results apply to families of networks and circuits with constant depth, and cover all common activation functions. They hold in both uniform and non-uniform settings. Constant depth is therefore part of the stated scope of the characterization. The contribution is theoretical: it connects GNN expressivity to arithmetic-circuit expressivity exactly within that scope, providing a shared language for describing the computational power of these graph architectures.
neurips-2024-graph-neural-networks-and-a.tldr: The paper exactly relates constant-depth GNN expressivity to real arithmetic circuits, with activation functions corresponding to circuit gates.

paragraphs: The manifold hypothesis says that high-dimensional data lies on or near a lower-dimensional geometric surface. This paper asks which properties of that surface make neural networks efficiently learnable. It focuses on whether geometric restrictions, including constraints on curvature and regularity, are enough to overcome established computational barriers to learning.

The authors prove hardness results even when the input manifold has bounded curvature. They extend arguments from Boolean-input learning to geometric inputs in both statistical-query and cryptographic settings. Thus, restricting curvature alone does not remove the learning difficulties covered by those results. Low-dimensional geometric structure needs more specific assumptions to support the positive conclusion investigated here.

The paper also identifies a learnable regime: additional assumptions on manifold volume allow a guarantee through a simple interpolation argument. Manifolds that can be reliably reconstructed by manifold learning provide notable examples within that regime. Finally, the authors empirically explore intermediate cases with heterogeneous features associated with real-world data. The overall contribution separates geometric assumptions that still permit hardness from stronger conditions sufficient for learnability.
neurips-2024-hardness-of-learning-neural.tldr: Bounded manifold curvature still permits learning hardness, while additional volume assumptions can guarantee learnability through interpolation.

paragraphs: Text-conditioned diffusion models can produce high-quality images while showing limited variety across samples from the same description. The paper highlights this issue particularly when classifier-free guidance is strong. Kaleido addresses it by introducing generated intermediate representations between the original caption and the image-generation process.

An autoregressive language model encodes the caption and generates latent variables that provide additional guidance to the diffusion model. The authors investigate several discrete forms for these variables: textual descriptions, detection bounding boxes, object blobs, and visual tokens. These intermediates enrich and diversify the conditions supplied to the image generator, allowing one caption to lead to different guided outputs.

Experiments show greater diversity among images generated from a given description while maintaining high image quality. The generated images also closely follow the latent guidance. That finding matters because the intermediate representations serve two related purposes: they introduce variation and provide a way to direct the result. Kaleido therefore connects diversity improvements with controllability through the same generated conditioning stage.
neurips-2024-kaleido-diffusion-improving.tldr: Kaleido generates intermediate latent guidance from captions to increase diffusion-image diversity while maintaining quality and control.

paragraphs: Learning embeddings for a large directed graph usually requires sampling its adjacency matrix because inspecting every entry is impractical. The paper asks whether known hierarchical structure can identify a smaller set of entries that still uniquely determines the graph. Its setting is transitively closed directed acyclic graphs, a structured class of hierarchical relations.

The authors develop a framework for finding the entries needed to distinguish one such graph from every other graph in that class. They provide an explicit algorithm that computes a provably minimal set. This turns training-example selection into a problem guided by what information is sufficient to identify the hierarchy, rather than relying only on general sampling.

Experiments show that embedding models can learn more efficiently and perform better with these selected entries, provided their energy function has an appropriate inductive bias. Tests on synthetic hierarchies and a larger real-world taxonomy show improved convergence under resource constraints, with training examples reduced by as much as 99%. The guarantee concerns minimal identifying information, while the training benefits additionally depend on a suitably structured model.
neurips-2024-learning-representations-fo.tldr: A provably minimal identifying set for transitively closed DAGs enables more efficient embedding training when the model has an appropriate inductive bias.

paragraphs: Graph learning often faces scarce labels, yet methods intended to reduce label dependence can still require task-specific fine-tuning. TEA-GLM explores using an instruction-tuned LLM as a predictor that transfers across graph datasets and tasks. Its central challenge is making graph representations usable by a language model without tuning the LLM itself.

The framework first pretrains a graph neural network while aligning its representations with the LLM's token embeddings. It then trains a linear projector to convert GNN representations into a fixed number of graph token embeddings. A unified instruction supports graph tasks at different levels, including node classification and edge-level link prediction. Together, these components provide a common interface between graph structure and language-model prediction.

Experiments on unseen datasets and tasks report state-of-the-art performance relative to other methods that use LLMs as predictors. The zero-shot capability concerns transfer to those unseen settings; the GNN and projector are trained components of the framework. The results support representation alignment as a way to make a fixed LLM useful for multiple graph-learning tasks.
neurips-2024-llms-as-zero-shot-graph-lea.tldr: TEA-GLM aligns graph representations with LLM token embeddings to support zero-shot prediction across unseen graph datasets and tasks.

paragraphs: A medical digital twin is a mathematical simulation intended to reproduce features of a patient's physiological condition. Such a model can support virtual exploration of disease processes and hypothetical interventions. Med-Real2Sim focuses on estimating the parameters of these models using noninvasive patient data, connecting observable measurements to the physiological process that could have generated them.

The authors formulate this estimation as a composite inverse problem and use its structure to design a self-supervised learning procedure. First, a neural network learns a differentiable simulator of a physiological process. It is then trained to reconstruct physiological measurements from noninvasive modalities, with the physical equations learned during pretraining constraining this second stage.

The application is cardiac hemodynamics: the method identifies digital twins using echocardiogram videos. The authors demonstrate utility for unsupervised disease detection and simulated clinical trials. The contribution links noninvasive observations with a physics-informed simulation model, so the resulting representation can support both reconstruction of physiological measurements and exploration of outcomes within a virtual setting.
neurips-2024-med-real2sim-non-invasive-m.tldr: Med-Real2Sim uses physics-informed self-supervised learning to estimate cardiac digital twins from noninvasive echocardiogram videos.

paragraphs: In multi-label learning, an example can belong to several classes simultaneously. Standard formulations assume that the labels encountered during testing are the same ones available during training. This paper studies an open setting, where previously unknown labels can emerge during testing, making recognition more complicated than assigning labels from a fixed list.

The proposed method, SLAN, uses sub-labeling information enriched by structure in the feature space. Its recognition mechanism differentiates that information from the holistic supervision associated with an example. The key idea is to use information within the multi-label structure, together with relationships in the learned features, to help recognize the presence of unknown labels.

Experiments on several datasets support SLAN's effectiveness for multi-label open-set recognition. The contribution brings together two requirements: predicting labels when examples can have several of them, and recognizing unknown labels in a changing environment. By explicitly studying that combination, the paper broadens the prediction problem beyond the closed-set assumption that all relevant test-time classes were already represented during training.
neurips-2024-multi-label-open-set-recogn.tldr: SLAN uses sub-labeling information and feature-space structure to recognize unknown labels in multi-label prediction.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can become more expressive when subgraphs exchange information, including through higher-order messages. To account faithfully for local structures such as cycles, their local operations must respect the symmetries of the local environment. Here, that means being equivariant to its automorphism group: the operation must respond consistently to those structural symmetries.

Constructing these operations separately for each subgraph is generally impractical because it requires determining many automorphism groups. Schur Nets uses spectral graph theory to bypass that step. The method constructs a basis for equivariant operations directly from the graph Laplacian, providing the required building blocks without explicitly enumerating the local symmetry group.

The approach makes local graph structure available to higher-order neural architectures through a more tractable construction of symmetry-respecting operations. The authors show performance improvements on some standard GNN benchmarks. Those results support the usefulness of the construction in the tested settings, while the methodological contribution is the direct route from the Laplacian to equivariant operations for local environments.
neurips-2024-schur-nets-exploiting-local.tldr: Schur Nets constructs local equivariant graph operations from the Laplacian without explicitly determining automorphism groups.

paragraphs: Diffusion sampling normally generates an output through a sequence of refinement steps, making latency depend on many consecutive model evaluations. Self-Refining Diffusion Samplers aim to reduce that waiting time by using additional parallel computation while retaining sample quality. The approach draws on Parareal, a numerical method for solving differential equations in parallel across time.

SRDS first produces a quick, rough sample estimate. It then refines that estimate through parallel Parareal iterations along the diffusion trajectory. The method is guaranteed to accurately solve the ordinary differential equation and converge to the serial solution. Its structure also supports batched inference and pipelining, creating opportunities to run work concurrently across the sampling process.

Experiments with pretrained diffusion models show that refinement can converge early enough to reduce the steps needed to produce a sample. Reported speedups reach 1.7-fold on a 25-step StableDiffusion-v2 benchmark and 4.3-fold on longer trajectories. The practical trade-off is additional parallel compute for lower latency, with convergence to the serial solution providing the method's theoretical foundation.
neurips-2024-self-refining-diffusion-sam.tldr: SRDS uses parallel refinement along diffusion trajectories to reduce generation latency while converging to the serial solution.

paragraphs: SG-Nav addresses zero-shot object navigation: deciding where to search for a target object using observations of an environment. Earlier approaches described nearby objects to an LLM, leaving out broader scene context. This framework represents the observed environment as a 3D scene graph that records relationships among objects, groups, and rooms.

A hierarchical reasoning prompt guides the LLM through the graph's nodes and edges to infer a likely goal location. This gives the decision process access to relationships at several scales, rather than only a list of nearby items. The graph also supports a re-perception mechanism that allows the navigation system to correct perception errors.

Across MP3D, HM3D, and RoboTHOR, the authors report success-rate improvements of more than 10% over previous state-of-the-art zero-shot methods, alongside an explainable decision process. They also report outperforming supervised object-navigation methods on MP3D and describe this as a first for zero-shot navigation to their knowledge. The findings support structured scene context as useful both for search decisions and for revisiting mistaken observations.
neurips-2024-sg-nav-online-3d-scene-grap.tldr: SG-Nav uses a hierarchical 3D scene graph to guide LLM-based object search and support correction of perception errors.

paragraphs: Visual place recognition matches images to locations, supporting applications such as robot localization and augmented reality. Global feature aggregation methods such as NetVLAD can handle viewpoint changes, but many clusters produce large descriptors. Their learned cluster centers can also become unsuitable when deployment images differ from the training domain.

SuperVLAD removes cluster centers and uses far fewer clusters, with four given as an example. This simplifies aggregation while aiming to improve transfer across domains. The authors also introduce ghost clusters that participate in the method but are excluded from the final output. This produces a one-cluster descriptor with the same dimensionality as GeM pooling, while achieving notably better performance in their evaluation.

With a transformer backbone, experiments suggest better domain generalization than NetVLAD using substantially fewer parameters. SuperVLAD also exceeds state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks with lower-dimensional features. The results connect a simpler aggregation design to both compact representations and stronger recognition across differing data domains, addressing two practical pressures in large-scale place recognition.
neurips-2024-supervlad-compact-and-robus.tldr: SuperVLAD removes cluster centers and reduces cluster counts to produce compact place-recognition descriptors with improved domain generalization.

paragraphs: TOPA explores how to prepare a language model for video understanding without pretraining it on real videos. The motivation is that video complexity and inefficient language supervision make existing web video-text data difficult to use effectively. The method instead creates a textual training stage that imitates the sequential structure of video.

An advanced LLM generates sequences of textual frames and corresponding annotations. These textual videos are encoded as sequences of CLIP text features and used to pre-align a language-only LLM. CLIP provides the bridge to real video: its alignment of image and text modalities allows textual feature sequences to serve as counterparts to sequences of image features.

Experiments include zero-shot evaluation and fine-tuning across video-understanding tasks. Without training on video data, TOPA-Llama2-13B achieves 51.0% Top-1 accuracy on Egoschema, a long-form video-understanding benchmark. The authors report that this exceeds previous video-text pretraining approaches and is competitive with recent GPT-3.5-based video agents. The findings support synthetic textual sequences as useful preparation for processing real video representations.
neurips-2024-topa-extending-large-langua.tldr: TOPA prepares LLMs for video understanding using synthetic textual frame sequences and CLIP alignment, without real-video pretraining.

paragraphs: Nonlinear recurrent neural networks appear difficult to evaluate in parallel because their states depend on earlier states. DEER addresses this by treating the full state sequence as a fixed-point problem and solving it with a parallel version of Newton's method. However, its computation scales cubically with state size, and the solver can suffer from numerical instability.

This paper introduces two changes to address those obstacles. First, quasi-Newton approximations reduce computational demands. The authors show that these approximations converge comparably to Newton's method while using less memory and running faster. This targets the cost that makes the original approach difficult to apply to larger recurrent states.

Second, the ELK approach connects the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm with Kalman smoothing. That connection provides a way to stabilize Newton's method while retaining efficient parallel computation through parallelized smoothing algorithms. Across several experiments, the two innovations enable evaluation of nonlinear RNNs at larger scales and with greater stability. The contribution improves the practical behavior of the fixed-point solver used to parallelize recurrent evaluation.
neurips-2024-towards-scalable-and-stable.tldr: Quasi-Newton approximations and Kalman-smoothing-based stabilization make parallel nonlinear RNN evaluation more scalable and numerically stable.

paragraphs: The Fisher information matrix describes local geometry in a neural network's parameter space and supports methods for understanding and optimizing networks. Computing it is expensive, so practitioners often estimate only its diagonal entries using randomness. This paper examines how reliable two popular estimators are and what governs the number of samples they need.

The analysis centers on estimator variance, which affects both accuracy and sample complexity. The authors derive bounds on the variances and work out their implications for neural networks used in regression and classification. They combine analytical results with numerical studies to examine the trade-offs between the two estimators across these settings.

A central finding is that the relevant variance depends on nonlinearity with respect to different groups of parameters. Consequently, the uncertainty of a diagonal Fisher estimate is connected to how the network depends on the parameters being examined. The paper makes these dependencies explicit, showing why variance deserves attention when selecting and interpreting an estimator rather than treating every diagonal estimate as equally reliable.
neurips-2024-trade-offs-of-diagonal-fish.tldr: The paper analyzes variance trade-offs between two diagonal Fisher estimators and shows their dependence on parameter-group nonlinearity.

paragraphs: Adapting large vision Transformers to new tasks can require updating many parameters. Visual prompt tuning offers a more parameter-efficient route, but performance can deteriorate when pretraining and adaptation datasets differ substantially. Visual Fourier Prompt Tuning addresses this gap by changing the information represented in the learned prompts.

VFPT incorporates the Fast Fourier Transform into prompt embeddings so that adaptation considers both spatial and frequency-domain information. The design draws inspiration from human visual cognition and is presented as a simple way to adapt large Transformer-based vision models. Its central idea is to enrich prompt representations while keeping the number of adaptation parameters small.

The authors report stronger performance across the evaluated datasets and improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on two benchmarks. On VTAB-1k, they report 73.20% mean accuracy while using 0.57% of the model's parameters. These results support the usefulness of combining spatial and frequency information within prompts, particularly for the paper's motivating challenge of adapting a pretrained model when the target data differs from its original training data.
neurips-2024-visual-fourier-prompt-tunin.tldr: VFPT adds Fourier information to visual prompts to improve parameter-efficient adaptation across differing datasets.

paragraphs: WorkArena++ evaluates whether autonomous web agents can apply planning and reasoning to realistic workplace tasks. Language models may appear capable of reasoning from instructions, but carrying that ability through an entire workflow remains a separate question. The benchmark focuses on enterprise knowledge work, where useful agents must combine several abilities while completing tasks.

It contains 682 tasks corresponding to workflows routinely performed by knowledge workers. These tasks assess planning, problem-solving, logical and arithmetic reasoning, information retrieval, and contextual understanding. The authors evaluate state-of-the-art language models and vision-language models, alongside human workers. Their empirical study reveals several challenges for models attempting to function as useful workplace assistants.

The contribution also includes a mechanism for generating thousands of ground-truth observation and action traces. Those traces can be used to fine-tune existing models, connecting the evaluation resource with a potential source of training data. WorkArena++ therefore provides both a test of autonomous task execution and material for developing agents that can handle the combinations of reasoning and interaction required by workplace workflows.
neurips-2024-workarena-towards-compositi.tldr: WorkArena++ tests web agents on 682 realistic workplace tasks and can generate ground-truth interaction traces for model fine-tuning.
